cards.title: Scope cookies with Domain and consider subdomain isolation for your store
cards.summary: Cookies are shared across subdomains by default only when you set Domain; treat each host as isolated unless you deliberately widen scope.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether login sessions on your shop subdomain should be visible to other hosts you control (blog, help center, marketing site).

cards.title: Treat cookie Path as broken and design defenses without it
cards.summary: Path was meant to limit a cookie to a URL prefix, but a page under another path can read it if you can reach its DOM; do not rely on it for isolation.
cards.use_when: Evaluating whether path-scoped cookies protect a store's admin panel, embedded login, or a differently-scoped part of a site.

cards.title: Don't rely on browser session cookies to expire on close
cards.summary: Session restoration means browsers often keep what the spec says should be cleared on close; set an explicit expiry.
cards.use_when: Configuring how long a customer's login or cart cookie should persist on your storefront.

cards.title: Scope agent and tool access with the same principle as cookies
cards.summary: Any token or credential your automation uses behaves like a session cookie — scope it, store it server-side, and make it revocable.
cards.use_when: Designing credentials and permissions for ecommerce automations: price updates, inventory sync, order operations, customer-data access, marketing tool integrations.

cards.title: Cookie Path Is Not a Security Boundary
cards.summary: Cookie path restrictions are not a reliable security mechanism; always set path to root and rely on domain scoping and other attributes instead.
cards.use_when: Configuring session or authentication cookies for a storefront, admin panel, or customer account area, and deciding what scope and attributes each cookie should carry.

cards.title: Set Secure, HttpOnly and SameSite on Session Cookies
cards.summary: Configure session cookies with Secure, HttpOnly, SameSite, and an explicit expiry so ambient authority cannot be abused cross-site.
cards.use_when: Implementing or hardening login, cart, and session cookies for an ecommerce store, including when migrating to HTTPS or reviewing an existing Express/Node cookie configuration.

cards.title: Convert Cookie Exfiltration to a Defensive Recognition Checklist
cards.summary: Understanding when a browser will attach a cookie to a request lets you identify which storefront endpoints are vulnerable to ambient-authority abuse.
cards.use_when: Reviewing state-changing storefront or admin endpoints (cart mutations, order creation, address or email changes, refunds, password reset) for cross-site request exposure.

cards.title: Prefer Tokens Over Ambient Cookie Authority for State Changes
cards.summary: Reduce reliance on ambient cookie authority for sensitive actions by requiring an explicit per-request token, since browsers attach cookies automatically.
cards.use_when: Designing defensive controls for high-value ecommerce operations such as placing orders, changing stored payment methods, issuing refunds, or editing admin permissions.

cards.title: SameSite Lax versus Strict: Choose by Funnel Impact
cards.summary: Select SameSite policy by weighing cross-site abuse protection against legitimate embedded and referral flows your store depends on.
cards.use_when: Deciding the SameSite setting for storefront session cookies when your site relies on embedded widgets, affiliate links, email campaign links, or third-party checkout embeds.

cards.title: Why Cross-Site POSTs Still Reach Your Endpoints
cards.summary: Forms are a legacy exception to the same-origin policy, so a cross-site page can submit a valid form to your server and the browser will attach the victim's cookies.
cards.use_when: Assessing whether a hidden cross-site form could trigger a state change on your order, account, or admin endpoints even though modern fetch requests would be blocked.

cards.title: Same-Origin Policy: What It Allows, Blocks and Leaves Open
cards.summary: The same-origin policy blocks cross-origin DOM access and response reading but permits embedding, navigation and resource loading, so map your storefront's cross-origin interactions against that boundary.
cards.use_when: Reviewing storefront widgets, embeds, iframes, third-party scripts, and CDN resource references to understand what cross-origin behavior is expected and what would be a vulnerability.

cards.title: Replace legacy document.domain relaxation with explicit messaging
cards.summary: Treat legacy origin relaxation as migration work rather than a new storefront integration pattern.
cards.use_when: Evaluating whether a legacy storefront, admin subdomain, or partner integration can rely on document.domain to share cookies or DOM access across subdomains.

cards.title: Attribute a Hijacked Session to the Right Threat Level
cards.summary: Evaluate what a stolen or forged session can actually do, because the same cross-site request is far more damaging against an admin than against a shopper.
cards.use_when: Prioritizing which ecommerce sessions to protect most tightly and where to require re-authentication, extra confirmation, or a second factor.

cards.title: Short Expiry With Rolling Renewal for Session Cookies
cards.summary: Set a modest cookie lifetime and renew it on each visit so legitimate users stay logged in while a stolen session has a bounded useful window.
cards.use_when: Choosing session and persistent-login cookie lifetimes for a storefront, balancing shopper convenience against the exposure window if a session is compromised.

cards.title: Inspect Request Origin with Security Headers During Testing
cards.summary: Use browser-provided request origin metadata to confirm how a request was triggered, so you can validate defences like SameSite against your actual attacker surface.
cards.use_when: Debugging why a SameSite or CSRF defence appears not to work, and confirming whether the browser is classifying a request as same-site or cross-site for your store.

cards.title: Never Use document.domain to Relax Same-Origin Policy
cards.summary: document.domain opt-in lets any attacker page on the same registrable domain cross origin boundaries, so treat it as a forbidden pattern.
cards.use_when: Auditing storefront or admin front-end code for cross-subdomain communication (e.g. shop.example.com talking to checkout.example.com) and deciding whether document.domain is acceptable.

cards.title: Use postMessage for Cross-Origin Page Communication
cards.summary: The postMessage API is the sanctioned way for cooperating origins to exchange messages, replacing the old fragment-identifier hack.
cards.use_when: Building or reviewing legitimate cross-origin communication in an ecommerce flow, e.g. a checkout iframe talking to the parent storefront, an embedded payment widget, or a third-party upsell frame.

cards.title: Always Specify targetOrigin When Posting Messages
cards.summary: Omitting the destination origin in postMessage leaks data to any page that manages to embed or reference your window.
cards.use_when: Reviewing any code on an account page, login helper or checkout frame that posts user data such as a name or session detail to a parent window.

cards.title: Validate event.origin on Every Message Listener
cards.summary: A message listener without an origin check accepts forged data from any page that holds a window reference, enabling spoofed user data.
cards.use_when: Hardening storefront frames that receive data such as logged-in status, cart contents, coupon codes or shipping details from a parent or sibling origin.

cards.title: Prevent Clickjacking on Checkout and Account Pages
cards.summary: If your site can be framed, an attacker overlays invisible elements and turns a visitor's click into a purchase, bid or account action.
cards.use_when: Reviewing whether a checkout, buy-now, one-click order, subscription cancel or account settings page should refuse to render inside a third-party frame.

cards.title: Set SameSite on Session Cookies to Stop Ambient Cross-Site Requests
cards.summary: Cross-site image, form and frame requests silently carry a visitor's cookies unless the session cookie is scoped with SameSite.
cards.use_when: Configuring authentication and cart-session cookies so cross-site requests from third-party pages cannot act as the logged-in shopper.

cards.title: Do Not Rely on the Referer Header for Access Control
cards.summary: Referer-based defences break under caching, referrer-policy opt-outs and legitimate unknown referrers.
cards.use_when: Considering blocking requests to product images, downloads, coupon pages or account resources based on where the request appears to come from.

cards.title: Treat Referrer Policy Settings as a Store-Level Trade-off
cards.summary: Choosing a referrer policy balances analytics, partner attribution and leaking private URLs.
cards.use_when: Setting or reviewing the referrer policy on storefront pages, order confirmations, customer dashboards or shared cart links.

cards.title: Treat Cross-Origin Script and Style Embeds as Full Trust
cards.summary: Scripts, stylesheets, images and fonts from other origins can be embedded by default, but an embedded script executes with your page's authority.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to load third-party JavaScript, CSS, fonts or pixels on product pages, checkout or account pages.

cards.title: Prevent Cross-Site Script Inclusion Leakage of JSON Endpoints
cards.summary: Endpoints that return JSON as a script-compatible response can be read cross-origin when loaded via a script tag.
cards.use_when: Reviewing API or data endpoints on a store that return buyer data, pricing tiers, inventory or account details and may be fetchable as scripts.

cards.title: Do Not Trust Cookie Path Scoping as an Origin Boundary
cards.summary: Cookies and the same-origin policy are different, mismatched models, so path scoping and subdomain scoping are weaker than they look.
cards.use_when: Designing cookie scope for a store with several subdomains, such as www, account and checkout, or auditing an existing cookie configuration.

cards.title: Bound Validation of Cross-Origin Flows to Owned Environments
cards.summary: Hands-on verification of frame and message behaviour belongs in local test setups with two controlled origins, not on live third-party sites.
cards.use_when: Prototyping or regression-testing cross-origin communication in a store's checkout or account flow before shipping postMessage or frame changes.

cards.title: Prevent Clickjacking with Frame-Ancestors Header
cards.summary: Use the Content-Security-Policy frame-ancestors directive (or legacy X-Frame-Options) to stop competitors and attackers embedding your storefront in a frame and overlaying invisible buttons.
cards.use_when: Hardening your storefront or admin dashboard against clickjacking, e.g. when a third party could overlay a hidden add-to-cart or account action over an enticing button.

cards.title: Reject Cross-Site Form Submissions Using Origin Header
cards.summary: Check the Origin header against an allow list to block form POSTs from other sites; this does not stop request forgery but prevents the request from being accepted.
cards.use_when: Protecting storefront or checkout endpoints that accept form POSTs, such as changing an account email, applying a promo code, or placing an order, from being forged by a third-party page.

cards.title: Protect private ecommerce media with authorization or scoped links
cards.summary: Distinguish private customer assets from public assets whose bandwidth needs protection.
cards.use_when: Serving images such as user avatars, customer-uploaded photos, downloadable receipts, or paid content where hotlinking or leaking would cost bandwidth or expose private data.

cards.title: Choose the Right Tool for Each Cross-Site Boundary Question
cards.summary: A decision framework mapping the same-origin questions (can A link to B, embed B, read B's data, submit forms, steal images/scripts) to reliable vs unreliable defenses.
cards.use_when: Architecting storefront integrations, embedded widgets, third-party scripts, or any cross-origin data sharing and needing to know which control actually holds.

cards.title: Kill Cross-Site Scripting by Escaping User Data at Output
cards.summary: Treat all user-supplied strings as data by HTML-escaping them before inserting them into your page, and consider the limits of blacklists.
cards.use_when: Building any storefront page that reflects user input, such as a search results page, a personalized welcome based on a URL parameter, or a product review display.

cards.title: Why Cross-Site Scripting Is Worse Than Clickjacking for Your Store
cards.summary: Understand the attacker's goal — running code in your origin so they act as a logged-in customer — before choosing defenses.
cards.use_when: Prioritizing remediation when you discover a stored or reflected input vulnerability on a customer-facing page like a profile, review, or search results page.

cards.title: Avoid JSONP for Partner Data; Prefer Headers or Proxy
cards.summary: JSONP lets a cooperating server hand you cross-origin data wrapped in a callback, but it grants that origin execution context on your page — consider safer alternatives.
cards.use_when: Deciding how a storefront should read JSON from a partner or internal API that lives on a different origin, especially when the data varies per logged-in user.

cards.title: Layer CSRF defenses on authenticated store actions
cards.summary: Use framework CSRF protection, origin checks and appropriate cookies together for state-changing requests.
cards.use_when: Configuring session cookie attributes for a storefront so cross-site pages can't trigger authenticated actions like account changes or a placed order against a logged-in customer.

cards.title: Treat Script and Image Inclusion as Best-Effort, Not Secure
cards.summary: Blocking hotlinked scripts and images is about bandwidth, not confidentiality, and Referer-based blocking is explicitly unreliable.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether and how to stop other sites embedding your images, stylesheets or JavaScript (e.g. a signature animation or theme asset they are stealing).

cards.title: Make Store Input Fields Untrusted by Default
cards.summary: The root condition for both XSS and SQL injection is mixing untrusted customer input with code, so treat every input field as a potential injection vector.
cards.use_when: Reviewing storefront and back-office features that accept customer text — signup fields, search boxes, review forms, support messages, profile/bio fields — before launch.

cards.title: Automate Defensive Controls Across All Store Pages
cards.summary: Anti-framing and output-escaping controls should be applied consistently at the site or framework level, not page-by-page where gaps appear.
cards.use_when: Rolling out security headers and escaping after an audit reveals inconsistent coverage across your storefront's templates.

cards.title: Treat all client-supplied data as untrusted input
cards.summary: Any value from URLs, form fields, headers or profile data must be escaped before insertion into HTML or JavaScript, because client data can never be trusted.
cards.use_when: Designing or reviewing any storefront feature that echoes user input — search terms, review text, profile names, wishlist labels, coupon codes, or URL parameters — back into the page.

cards.title: Escape user data inside HTML element contexts
cards.summary: When inserting untrusted data between HTML tags, escape the left angle bracket, ampersand, and both quote characters to neutralize injected markup.
cards.use_when: Rendering user-supplied text into normal page regions such as review bodies, collection descriptions, order notes, or any block that is not a script, style, comment or tag name.

cards.title: Always quote HTML attribute values you build
cards.summary: Unquoted attributes let browsers treat many characters as ending the value, so never build storefront attributes without surrounding quotes.
cards.use_when: Generating HTML snippets for product images, alt text, srcsets, data attributes, or any element whose attribute values include dynamic store data.

cards.title: High-power attributes need value validation, not just escaping
cards.summary: Attributes like src and href can execute or load attacker-controlled content even when quotes are correctly escaped, so validate the URL itself.
cards.use_when: Any storefront flow that lets a user or merchant supply a URL for an image, link, iframe, or script — user avatars, custom collection banners, affiliate links, or rich-text product descriptions.

cards.title: Reject data: and javascript: URLs in user-supplied links
cards.summary: data: and javascript: URLs can execute arbitrary code, so block them wherever users can supply a link or source.
cards.use_when: Building any feature that accepts a user-submitted link or image source — user-generated content, curated wishlists, third-party product feeds, or rich product description editors.

cards.title: Escaping alone fails inside inline event handlers and JS strings
cards.summary: When user data sits inside an inline handler (onclick) or a script string, you need JavaScript-level escaping in addition to HTML escaping, or break out is possible.
cards.use_when: Generating trigger text, analytics labels, or inline event handlers that embed store data, or embedding a user string inside a <script> variable.

cards.title: Avoid pages where user data passes through nested parsers
cards.summary: Layered contexts (HTML attribute to JavaScript string to eval-like call) require multiple correctly-ordered escapes and are extremely error-prone, so avoid the pattern.
cards.use_when: Designing features where store data flows through an HTML attribute, then a JavaScript string, then a dynamic execution call (e.g. rich-text widgets, custom button scripts, or analytics configuration).

cards.title: Only HTML element text and quoted attributes are reliably escapable
cards.summary: Several HTML contexts (comments, tag names, script bodies as plain text) cannot be escaped safely, so refuse to insert user data there.
cards.use_when: Reviewing or designing any template or editor where store or customer data could land in a comment, in a tag name, or directly in a script body.

cards.title: Recognise reflected versus stored XSS and prioritise accordingly
cards.summary: Reflected XSS lives in the request, while stored XSS persists in your data and reaches every visitor regardless of the URL they use.
cards.use_when: Triageing vulnerability findings or designing storefront features: deciding where user data is stored (reviews, profiles, messages) versus only reflected in a response (search, filters).

cards.title: Escaping cannot defeat breakouts caused by a closing script tag
cards.summary: The HTML parser locates script tag boundaries before JavaScript parsing, so a literal closing script tag anywhere in a script breaks out regardless of string escaping.
cards.use_when: Reviewing any storefront or checkout page where user data or third-party content is embedded in a script, or when evaluating page-builder widgets that inject sequences into scripts.

cards.title: Blacklist filtering of tag names fails against forgiving HTML parsers
cards.summary: HTML parsers are deliberately lenient, accepting many syntax variations that bypass tag-name blacklists.
cards.use_when: Evaluating any input sanitisation that tries to block specific tags or words in customer reviews, product descriptions, or rich-text fields.

cards.title: Beware DOM-injected globals via user-controlled element IDs
cards.summary: The DOM exposes elements with IDs as global JavaScript variables, so letting users choose an ID can let them inject or override variables your script depends on.
cards.use_when: Designing features that assign element IDs from user input, such as personalised widgets, review anchors, or per-customer page components.

cards.title: Use data URLs for small inline assets, not large ones
cards.summary: Data URLs can inline small images or stylesheets into a page to save an HTTP round trip, but they cannot be cached and bloat the document.
cards.use_when: Choosing whether to inline small storefront assets such as icons or logos into the page or CSS, versus serving them as separate requests.

cards.title: Fix XSS with Context-Aware Output Encoding
cards.summary: Encode untrusted values separately for each output context (HTML body, attribute, JavaScript string, URL) rather than escaping once at input.
cards.use_when: Reviewing or briefing developers on your storefront's product review fields, search results pages, or any template that echoes customer-supplied content.

cards.title: Treat XSS Filtering Browser Features as Unreliable
cards.summary: Built-in reflected-XSS filters can be bypassed and even aid attackers, so do not count on them as your storefront's XSS defense.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether browser-level XSS filtering removes the need for server-side sanitization on your storefront's reflected input pages.

cards.title: Choose Between Content-Matched and Person-Targeted Ads
cards.summary: Content-based ad placement ties ad revenue to page quality; person-level tracking decouples ad value from content and shifts spend toward cheap, low-quality pages.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether your store should buy content-matched placements (relevant publishers, category pages) or behavioral audiences, and understanding why cheap inventory may outperform contextually relevant inventory on cost.

cards.title: Plan for Third-Party Tags as Tracking Surfaces
cards.summary: A typical page loads around twenty third-party resources with tracking vantage, and roughly 70-80% of first-party URLs may be observable by one large analytics provider, per the cited census.
cards.use_when: Auditing your store's third-party script footprint or preparing a privacy review before adding another analytics, personalization or ad tag.

cards.title: Understand Cookies and Third-Party Cookie Exposure
cards.summary: Cookies store a server-issued identifier returned on subsequent requests; the decision to send them on third-party image and iframe requests is what enabled cross-site tracking.
cards.use_when: Reviewing how your store's session, cart persistence and embedded third-party content handle cookies.

cards.title: Treat HSTS as a Security Feature That Can Be Repurposed
cards.summary: HSTS tells browsers to refuse plaintext requests to a domain, but subdomain-level rules can be abused to encode per-user bits.
cards.use_when: Reviewing domain and subdomain configuration for your store, especially if you control or delegate many subdomains.

cards.title: Assess Fingerprinting Risk on Your Storefront Analytics
cards.summary: Fingerprinting identifies a browser by combining many semi-unique attributes without storing anything, so it survives cookie clearing and third-party cookie blocking.
cards.use_when: Evaluating whether removing third-party cookies actually reduces cross-site tracking of your store's visitors, or choosing an analytics approach for privacy-sensitive audiences.

cards.title: Recognize Font Enumeration and Why It Is Hard to Fix
cards.summary: Pages infer installed local fonts by measuring whether applying a candidate font changes an element's size, giving one entropy bit per unusual font.
cards.use_when: Evaluating a privacy-preserving analytics or anti-tracking approach that claims to neutralize fingerprinting, to check whether font enumeration is addressed.

cards.title: Treat Canvas and Audio Fingerprinting as Unpredictable APIs
cards.summary: Canvas and audio rendering produce slightly different output across hardware and drivers, which can be hashed into an identifier the user never sees.
cards.use_when: Understanding what browser-based fingerprinting can extract from visitors to your store, or assessing what a privacy tool must suppress.

cards.title: Audit Permissionless Hardware and Network APIs
cards.summary: Several APIs expose hardware and network characteristics without any permission prompt, giving every script on the page identifying data.
cards.use_when: Auditing third-party scripts on your store or judging how much identifying data your pages already leak by default.

cards.title: Treat Viewport Size as the Hardest Fingerprint to Fake
cards.summary: True visible window dimensions are difficult to spoof without breaking layout, making them among the most identifying browser attributes.
cards.use_when: Assessing how much identifying information your responsive storefront design indirectly exposes, or evaluating anti-fingerprinting tooling.

cards.title: Use Hashing Aggregation to Reason About Poisoning Fingerprints
cards.summary: Fingerprinting implementations typically hash many inputs into one combined value; corrupting one input can invalidate the whole fingerprint.
cards.use_when: Evaluating anti-fingerprinting approaches or deciding which single signal a protection should target when full masking is impractical.

cards.title: Account for Cookie Syncing Across Identifiers
cards.summary: Tracking consolidates multiple cookie identifiers into one person by matching them with fingerprint data when a cookie is new or unrecognized.
cards.use_when: Understanding why clearing cookies or blocking third-party cookies alone does not sever an existing cross-site profile of your store's visitors.

cards.title: Check New Tags for Identity-Linking Risk Before Adding
cards.summary: Any script with broad page access may join your visitors' identifiers to external profiles; review new store tools for this before shipping.
cards.use_when: Before adding a personalization, reviews, chat, A/B testing, or attribution vendor to your storefront.

cards.title: Set Up a Repeatable External Script Review
cards.summary: Consistent periodic review of embedded scripts, APIs used, and identifiers collected keeps tracking exposure from quietly expanding as the store changes.
cards.use_when: Scheduling a recurring privacy and security review of your ecommerce site, or onboarding a new developer to review standards.

cards.title: Browser API permission tiers for storefront feature planning
cards.summary: Browser APIs sit in tiers from unrestricted (DOM, downloads) through user-gesture-gated to permission-prompt and engagement-gated, and knowing the tier tells you what a storefront can do on page load versus after a user interaction.
cards.use_when: Deciding when a storefront can trigger clips, sound, fullscreen, vibration, clipboard or camera during PDP video, spin-to-win, or promotional widgets.

cards.title: UI denial-of-service patterns that can lock down a storefront session
cards.summary: A malicious or compromised page can override ordinary browser escape routes — back button, close-window shortcuts, context menus — and a commerce operator should know these exist as scareware and annoyance vectors, not as legitimate merchandising behavior.
cards.use_when: Auditing suspect third-party scripts, promo takeovers, or scareware landing pages that trap shoppers, and deciding what to add to a monitoring or content-review checklist.

cards.title: GET-request and CSRF exposure in storefront logout and account actions
cards.summary: State-changing actions reachable by a GET request can be triggered by any site embedding a matching image or link, so a storefront should keep logout, prefetch and account mutations behind POST plus SameSite cookies.
cards.use_when: Reviewing storefront endpoints for logout, cart mutation, wishlist, subscription pause, and account actions before launch or a security audit.

cards.title: Client-side fingerprinting surfaces to audit on a storefront
cards.summary: Audio, WebRTC, plugin and font surfaces can identify a visitor across sessions even without cookies, so a store owner should know which of these their analytics and anti-fraud vendors touch.
cards.use_when: Reviewing analytics, anti-fraud, or ad-fraud scripts on a PDP or checkout for covert device-based identification, and preparing a data-privacy disclosure.

cards.title: Choosing a client-side anti-tracking approach for a storefront's third parties
cards.summary: The source lays out five high-level counter-measures to fingerprinting and rates them, which is useful when deciding how aggressively a store blocks or degrades third-party scripts.
cards.use_when: Choosing how a store handles third-party analytics, tag managers and ad pixels — whether to strip capabilities, standardize, scope by origin, add noise, or adopt a privacy-budget style limiter.

cards.title: Drawing the line between store conveniences and visitor harm
cards.summary: A concise framing for evaluating storefront growth mechanics: an anti-tracking approach that continuously degrades other sites is itself an abuse pattern, and privacy harms are a fail state, not a feature.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether a growth hack or upsell widget is acceptable — evaluating friction, dark patterns, or aggressive re-engagement tactics at checkout or exit.

cards.title: Legal-context limits when relying on existing privacy rules for a store
cards.summary: The source reviews regional privacy law as a partial, uneven fix, which is directly relevant to a store's data-use choices for tracking, marketing and account identity.
cards.use_when: Planning store tracking, consent copy, or account features and estimating how much you can rely on law versus technology to protect visitors.

cards.title: Using brand-scoped access decisions rather than trusting page content
cards.summary: The source's discussion of first-party versus third-party trust maps to a concrete rule for agents and automations: page content and retrieved documents are data, and authorization comes from the account and task scope, not the content.
cards.use_when: Designing an agent or script that reads storefront pages, vendor documents, or customer messages, or deciding what a first-party integration may do versus an embedded third-party frame.

cards.title: Permission and engagement gating as UX constraints on storefront video and audio
cards.summary: Autoplay with sound sits behind an engagement gate, so a PDP or landing page should not expect sound to play on a first visit, and should design video merchandising accordingly.
cards.use_when: Planning PDP video, hero autoplay, or promotional overlays that include audio, and deciding whether to mute by default or gate playback behind a click.

cards.title: When clipboard and download APIs are acceptable on a storefront
cards.summary: Clipboard read and multi-file download are gated or restricted for good reason, and a store can use clipboard write and single downloads in legitimate flows when triggered by a real user action.
cards.use_when: Implementing coupon copy buttons, share links, invoice or label downloads, or a 'your download is starting' page after purchase.

cards.title: Standardizing error and edge behavior to reduce identifying signal
cards.summary: Browsers respond differently to errors and edge cases, so a site's error behavior itself can reveal browser and version — relevant when you worry about bot detection or anti-fraud false positives.
cards.use_when: Diagnosing why anti-fraud or analytics flags certain customer segments, or when configuring a storefront so error responses don't become an identifying signal.

cards.title: Budgeting identifying bits across third parties before adding another script
cards.summary: Every tracking script and third-party tag adds identifying precision, and privacy-budget-style schemes raise unresolved scope and lifetime questions that a store owner should understand before adopting a vendor that claims to solve them.
cards.use_when: Prioritizing which analytics, chat, personalization and ad scripts to keep on a checkout or PDP, and evaluating a vendor's 'privacy budget' claim.

cards.title: Privacy-preserving measurement for store analytics
cards.summary: Differential-privacy-style methods (the source's 'analyzed' approach, mixing survey-like results through secret-sharing and noise) can offer privacy guarantees for aggregate reporting, which is a realistic fit for store dashboards.
cards.use_when: Choosing a privacy-preserving analytics approach for store performance reporting, cohorts or vendor-shared benchmarks.

cards.title: Defend storefront links against tab nabbing (reverse tabnabbing)
cards.summary: Any outbound link that opens in a new tab can let the destination site navigate your customer's original store tab to a fake page, so add rel=noopener to external links.
cards.use_when: Auditing or building outbound links on a storefront, PDP, blog, help center, or email/chat share flow that opens partner, review, ad, or supplier links in a new tab.
